answer: On this Linux worktree the marketplace install/offline-import extractor (tools/marketplace/archive_extract.py via tools/marketplace/offline_import.py) fail-closes: relative traversal, nested pkg/../../ bypass of a pre-normalisation startswith('..') check, absolute paths, external symlinks, hardlinks, Windows device names (CON/NUL), and a 333333.3:1 zip bomb are rejected with zero files written inside or outside the intended root (verdicts REFUTED; each lands nowhere). A benign two-file archive extracts completely into dest. stdlib tarfile.extractall without filter writes ../ outside dest (negative control red). Device names are rejected by policy before create; Linux would otherwise write a regular file named CON, which is not a crash. Target verdicts: {'T1-relative-traversal': 'REFUTED', 'T2-absolute-path': 'REFUTED', 'T3-external-symlink': 'REFUTED', 'T4-hardlink': 'REFUTED', 'T5-device-name': 'REFUTED', 'T6-compression-ratio': 'REFUTED', 'T1b-nested-dotdot-pre-normalize-bypass': 'REFUTED'}.

question: Does the install/import path accept an archive containing ../ traversal entries, absolute paths, symlinks pointing outside the extraction root, or a Windows device name - and where does each land?

residual_unknowns.claim: On python >= 3.14 the stdlib tarfile data filter refuses the ../ member outright, so the naive-extraction bad state that NC-NAIVE-TAR-EXTRACTALL calibrates against is unrepresentable on this runtime; the control records that world instead of firing. Whether the import path would have failed closed against a REAL vulnerable stdlib is evidenced only by the six hostile-member rows, not by the naive control.
residual_unknowns.settling_experiment: Run the same matrix on a python < 3.12 host (or with tarfile extraction_filter='fully_trusted' scoped to the naive arm only): the naive extractall then lands the beacon outside dest and NC-NAIVE-TAR-EXTRACTALL fires. Not executable on this worktree's python 3.14.
